description:
Brazilian team interested in using NASA’s open data (Earth Observation, radar, and climate products) for solutions related to flood and landslide risks in Southern Brazil.

We focus on practical tools for alerts and information management. Looking for people in tech, data, design, and anyone with interest or experience in the topic.
summary: NISAR watched the Uruguay River rise and fall, pass after pass. Tipping Point turns NASA satellites into one answer for flood and landslide responders: when, where and who. At Uruguaiana, on the Argentine border, our index (GPM IMERG rain, SMAP soil moisture, NASADEM terrain) turned the region Critical on Sep 30, 2026, after three days of heavy rain upstream. Five days later, on Oct 5, the river reached flood stage and NISAR showed new water on both banks. NOAA's forecast from Sep 27 had pointed there 8 days ahead. Across nine L-band passes on two tracks, open water near the channel grew from 2 km² at low river to 36 km² at the crest and shrank as the river fell, tracking the official gauge (r = 0.92). About 98,000 people live on that floodplain. In Washington State (December 2025), clouds hid 93% of the area from optical satellites and a NISAR pass pair mapped 27.99 km² of flood candidates. We also showed why radar misses flooded towns: double bounce cancels the darkening. The index finds the right days, not yet the right streets. NISAR is how we check the streets.
details:
What it does

Tipping Point is one operations screen for anyone responding to floods and landslides, such as a municipal Civil Defense office. It answers three questions in order. Where is the ground about to fail? Where has radar seen new water? Who is affected?

- Live. Refreshes every 3 hours over Southern Brazil, with today's risk, three forecast days, OPERA flood candidates, the NISAR pass status and a ranked list of priority areas with the people exposed.

- Public Alerts. Area alerts in plain language. They are an experimental research product, not official warnings. Official alerts in Brazil come from Defesa Civil (SMS 40199).

- Replay. Past disasters day by day, with no look-ahead. Each day uses only the data and the forecast available that day.

NISAR time series: the river's dance

We followed the Uruguay River at Uruguaiana through nine NISAR L-band HH passes, from Sep 18 to Nov 5, 2026, on two descending tracks (010D and 082D). Combining the two tracks gave us a look every 5 to 7 days instead of every 12.

- Method. One fixed 30 × 30 km window. In each pass, open water is HH below −15 dB, kept only within 3 km of the permanent channel, in patches of 3 ha or more. We subtract the water present in almost every pass (the channel itself), so what remains is water that comes and goes.

- Result. That water went from 2 km² at low river (Sep 30) to 36 km² on the crest pass (Oct 12), then shrank as the river fell. Against the ANA gauge at Uruguaiana (station 77150000), water area and river stage correlate at r = 0.92 across the nine passes, and the relation holds inside each track (r = 0.92 on 010D, 5 passes; r = 0.94 on 082D, 4 passes).

- What it is not. This is single-pass water extent in a river corridor, not a gated before-and-after flood product. Our stricter automatic before/after check rejected the 010D pairs over Uruguaiana (see Validation). The two results are consistent. Along a large river, NISAR sees water extent clearly, while the change detector stays strict on purpose.

  • Four frames, one window. In an 18 × 18 km window over the flooded reach (track 082D, full coverage), new water was 1.8 km² on Sep 23 (river 5.5 m), 11.7 km² on Oct 5, the day the river passed flood stage (8.5 m), and 25.7 km² on Oct 17 near the crest (10.0 m). Our index had turned that same window Critical on Sep 30, using the live platform's map for that day.
  • Why the river is slow. The Uruguay River drains about 192,600 km² above Uruguaiana. The main rain pulse fell on the basin from Sep 27 to 29 (about 110 mm in three days, IMERG Early). The river barely moved until Oct 3, passed flood stage on Oct 5 and peaked at 10.02 m on Oct 16. A second pulse (about 79 mm, Oct 8 to 12) also fed that crest, so the crest is not only the rain the index saw on Sep 30.

How it works

- Tipping Point Index (TPI). A weighted geometric mean of three scores in \(0, 1\), with equal weights for now. Rain is GPM IMERG 3-day accumulation against each pixel's own P90, P95 and P99 climatology. Soil is SMAP L4 root-zone wetness. Terrain is NASADEM slope for landslides and a height-above-drainage proxy for floods. The index only reaches Critical (above 0.6) when all three agree.

- Forecast. The next three days extend observed rain with the NOAA GFS 0.25° forecast. This is our only non-NASA input, and every map label says so.

- Radar response. For each pair of NISAR passes, we detect new open water from the HH change (a drop of more than 3 dB to below a per-scene threshold, with a fixed −15 dB fallback for these BETA data), keep only low ground near rivers (height above drainage below 15 m), remove permanent water and keep patches of 3 ha or more. OPERA DSWx-S1 adds C-band water candidates, and OPERA DIST-ALERT-HLS adds landslide scar candidates once the cloud clears.

- NISAR never multiplies the index. The index runs every 6 hours and radar comes every few days. If NISAR were a factor in the product, a missing pass or a processing error would silently set the risk to zero. NISAR stays an independent check on where the water is.

- Impact. GPW v4.11 population inside the radar candidates and inside Critical areas, and VIIRS Black Marble night-light loss.

What NISAR shows, and why

- Calm floodwater acts like a mirror to radar. It reflects the L-band pulse away from the satellite, so new flooding appears as new dark patches.

- Radar passes through cloud, which is why it works when optical cannot. L-band (24 cm) also passes through leaves and is barely affected by rain.

- Flooded towns and forests behave differently. Water under walls or trunks bounces the pulse back to the satellite (double bounce), which cancels the darkening. A darkening-only detector misses that flooding. We tested this and it holds (next section).

Hypothesis tested: why radar misses flooded towns and forests

- What we saw. In Washington, our NISAR candidates caught only 13% of the new water in NASA OPERA's C-band map for the same days.

- Hypothesis. Double bounce cancels HH darkening in built-up and forested places.

- Test. Same NISAR pass pair (Dec 4 → Dec 16, 2025), OPERA flood split by MODIS land cover, HH change measured per class.

- Result, supported. Of the 60,936 OPERA flood pixels we missed, 45% are urban or forest, against 5% of the pixels we caught (8.6× enriched). Flooded open land darkened 2.72 dB on average, flooded urban land only 0.66 dB and flooded forest 0.18 dB. Recall is 24.7% on open land, 3.4% in towns and 1.3% in forest. A darkening-only rule misses exactly where people live.

- What it does not show. Flooded towns and forests did not turn clearly brighter. The double bounce cancels the darkening rather than reversing it, so closing the gap needs HV, texture or land-cover-aware detection.

What we learned about NISAR

- Water extent along big rivers is clear and repeatable. Nine passes on two tracks followed the Uruguaiana gauge (r = 0.92). Two tracks turn a 12-day revisit into a look every 5 to 7 days.

- Double bounce hides the flood where people live. 45% of what we missed in Washington was urban or forest land. Darkening alone is not enough in towns.

- Darkening is not flooding. At Uruguaiana, HH darkened over 15.7 km² of fields, probably rice irrigation, against 1.76 km² along the river. Terrain context (height above drainage, a corridor around the channel) is what turns a darkening map into a flood map.

- Every pair needs a gate. Our first live pair over Southern Brazil produced a 2.35 km² candidate strip on the swath edge, from passes with different acquisition modes. The live check now rejects mixed-mode pairs, threshold fallbacks and swath-edge patches.

- Thresholds on BETA data need care. On these early products the backscatter histogram is often not bimodal, so a per-scene threshold falls back to −15 dB. We report when that happens instead of hiding it.

- Landslides are still optical. No public NISAR interferogram (GUNW) spans our storms yet, so scar detection by coherence loss is untested and scars stay optical candidates.

Why L-band (NISAR), not just any radar

C-band radar (5.6 cm, behind NASA OPERA DSWx-S1) also sees open floodwater through cloud. It is our yardstick, not a competitor. NISAR's 24 cm L-band adds what this problem needs. It reaches water under vegetation canopy, keeps interferometric coherence over vegetated slopes for landslide work, and gives regular 12-day, dual-polarization (HH and HV) coverage of Brazil.

The future of NISAR for this problem

- Slow slope motion. Repeat-pass InSAR can measure slopes that creep before they fail. Fast rain-triggered shallow slides, like Rio Grande do Sul 2024, often give no warning.

- Soil moisture at high resolution. NISAR's \~200 m soil-moisture product could sharpen the soil score (SMAP is \~9 km), except under dense forest.

- Flooding under forest canopy. L-band passes through leaves, and HV can recover what HH darkening misses.

- Regular coverage of Brazil. Every municipality gets a radar look within days of a storm, whatever the weather.

Limitations

- NISAR's regular coverage of Southern Brazil began in late October 2026, and no live pass pair over our area has passed the checks yet. The Uruguaiana radar evidence is a replay.

- Our flood index did not flag the Washington river floods ahead of time, because it uses only local rain and rivers flood from rain upstream. An upstream-rain term is being tested.

- At the peak of an extreme event the rain score saturates and the index behaves like a terrain map. Rain tells when, terrain tells where.

- The index does not yet separate rain from snow. Thresholds are not yet calibrated for Brazil.

- IMERG and SMAP are about 10 km. The detail comes from terrain.

- Official warnings came before the index in both replays. Landslides are always candidates, never confirmed.
